stories.title: AI Is Rewiring the Office-Leasing Playbook
stories.excerpt: Much of the conversation around artificial intelligence and commercial real estate leasing has focused on whether AI will bring people back to the office. I think that’s the wrong question. The more important one is where AI companies are choosing to invest, hire and build because those decisions tell us far more about the next office cycle than return-to-office policies. After 20 years in commercial real estate, I’ve learned to be skeptical of bold predictions. I’ve watched plenty of cycles get oversold, but this one feels different, and the data tells us why. Start with where demand is actually concentrating. One submarket in San Francisco — the non-core central business district, including South of Market and Mission Bay — is responsible for 25 percent of all active AI office demand across the markets we track. San Francisco’s South Financial District accounts for another 16 percent, San Jose another 14 percent, and New York City’s Midtown South and Midtown another 11 percent and 8 percent, respectively. Ryan Masiello. These five submarkets across three markets account for nearly three-quarters of current AI square footage. National AI office demand is up 85 percent year-over-year, but, across the industry’s largest AI hubs, demand is up 179 percent. The story isn’t simply growth — it’s concentrated growth. Today’s market is fundamentally different from the last tech cycle. OpenAI raised $122 billion in February at an $840 billion valuation. Anthropic followed with $30 billion in a Series G at $380 billion. These aren’t 2022-era companies burning headcount against speculative valuations — both are scaling revenue far faster than headcount. Not only are current fundamentals far more sound, but the market opportunity is massive. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently stated that writing code is not the job of a software engineer. bullets: SF South of Market and Mission Bay account for 25% of all active AI office demand tracked
SF South Financial (16%), San Jose (14%), NYC Midtown South (11%) concentrate three-quarters of AI leasing
AI companies' location choices signal next office cycle more than return-to-office policies
stories.summary: AI companies are concentrating office leasing in specific high-tech submarkets rather than dispersing broadly. San Francisco Bay Area and select NYC neighborhoods account for nearly three-quarters of active AI office demand across tracked markets. The pattern reveals AI hiring and investment clusters driving demand geography independent of broader return-to-office trends.
stories.impact: Bay Area multifamily developers should monitor AI company hiring expansion in South of Market, Mission Bay, and San Jose—these tech employment centers drive young professional in-migration and rental demand. Conversely, traditional CBD office recovery may underperform, suggesting multifamily sites near AI-heavy submarkets and transit hubs will command premium demand and pricing in San Francisco, San Jose, and NYC.

stories.title: Legal AI Firm Sandstone Signs 14K-SF Lease at 141 East Houston Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-powered management platform designed to help law firms has signed an office lease on the Lower East Side, Commercial Observer has learned. AI platform Sandstone signed a five-year deal spanning 13,794 square feet on the entire third and fourth floors of East End Capital’s 141 East Houston Street, according to landlord broker Current Real Estate Advisors. Asking rent for the space was $93 per square foot. “This transaction is another example of what we’re continuing to see across the market,” Current’s Adam Henick, who represented the landlord alongside Rob Kluge, said in a statement. “We believed early on that delivering a newly built, fully furnished space with a premium level of finish would give the building a real competitive advantage, and this lease validates that strategy. When landlords invest in creating a best-in-class product, the market continues to reward it.” Newmark represented the tenant, which is relocating from 45 Main Street in Brooklyn, but the brokerage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. East End Capital developed the 63,000-square-foot property between Forsyth and Eldridge streets with Grandview Partners and Greg Kraut’s KPG Funds between 2020 and 2022 with designs by Roger Ferris + Partners. At the time, the project signaled a different kind of development pattern in the trendy enclave. Built on the site of the historic Sunshine Cinema, it’s unclear where the building stands in terms of occupancy, but it was around 50 percent full when the owners refinanced the property with a $79.6 million from Fortress in 2022. That same year, a private dining club that sold memberships through non-fungible tokens (remember those?) known as the Flyfish Club signed an 11,000-square-foot lease for three stories in the building. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sandstone AI (legal tech) leases 13.8K SF, relocates from Brooklyn to Lower East Side Manhattan
Five-year lease validates landlord strategy of newly built, fully furnished premium-finish buildings
AI platform leasing signals tenant demand for specialized, high-quality NYC office product
stories.summary: Sandstone, an AI-powered legal-services platform, signed a five-year, 13,794-square-foot lease at 141 East Houston Street on Manhattan's Lower East Side, relocating from Brooklyn. The transaction underscores landlord success in investing in newly constructed, fully furnished spaces with premium finishes. Broker commentary notes the lease validates market appetite for best-in-class office product tailored to tech and AI tenants.
stories.impact: AI-driven legal tech and professional services firms are pulling tenants out of outer boroughs into premium Manhattan locations, concentrating talent and capital in downtown/lower Manhattan. This reinforces demand for multifamily near Lower East Side, East Village, and downtown transit corridors to house in-migrating AI and fintech professionals at higher densities and rents.

stories.title: Mid-America Facilitates Sale of Iconic Lincoln Park Property
stories.excerpt: Mid-America Real Estate Corporation’s Investment Sales Group recently brokered the sale of Lincoln Park West, a 37,615-square-foot iconic retail asset located at the heart of Lincoln Park. The offering featured a durable rent roll and the opportunity to significantly add value through lease-up or adaptive reuse of the 19,531-square-foot second floor. Lincoln Park West is anchored by a tenant roster that includes PNC Bank, Starbucks, RJ Grunts, and Lincoln Park Preschool, collectively driving long-term stability given a weighted average lease term of 7 years. Lincoln Park West is situated at the base of a residential tower at the intersection of Lincoln Park West and Clark Street, on the ground level of a 16-story luxury condominium building. Mid-America Real Estate Corporation Senior Vice President George Ghattas, Principal Joe Girardi, and Senior Associate Patrick Corrigan served as the exclusive listing brokers on behalf of the seller, LLJ Ventures. The property was acquired by a local private investor. The post Mid-America Facilitates Sale of Iconic Lincoln Park Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lincoln Park West (37.6K SF mixed-use) sold by LLJ Ventures to local private investor; retail anchored by PNC, Starbucks, RJ Grunts
19.5K SF second-floor lease-up or adaptive-reuse upside identified; 7-year weighted average lease term provides stability

The second floor (19,531 SF) offers value-add through lease-up or adaptive reuse. The property sits at ground level of a 16-story luxury condominium building in Chicago's Lincoln Park neighborhood.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Property is retail-dominant with residential tower already built above; no signals of new residential supply, zoning shifts, or demand catalysts affecting Chicago multifamily market.

stories.title: Newport Resort Lists for $55M with Hotel Conversion Option
stories.excerpt: The Wellington Resort in Newport, RI has been listed for sale by Gustave White Sotheby’s International Realty, the Providence Business Journal reported. Located at the intersection of Thames Street and Wellington Avenue, the waterfront property is listed for $55 million. The resort at 551 Thames St. features 52 two-bedroom suites across four buildings. The Newport zoning board has given the resort approval for conversion of the property into 152 traditional one-bedroom hotel units.  Built in 1985, the resort previously operated as a timeshare, until the last timeshare agreements were dissolved in 2021. “This entitlement creates a rare opportunity to significantly increase density and unlock future development potential in one of Newport’s most coveted waterfront locations,” the listing said.  The 5.27-acre property is owned by Paolino Properties, a Providence-based real estate firm. Onsite amenities include indoor and outdoor swimming pools, tennis courts, a fitness center, and 208 parking spaces. The post Newport Resort Lists for $55M with Hotel Conversion Option appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Wellington Resort (Newport, RI) listed $55M; 5.27 acres, 52 two-bedroom suites, zoning approval for 152 hotel units

stories.summary: The Wellington Resort in Newport, Rhode Island, a 5.27-acre waterfront property with 52 two-bedroom suites, is listed for $55 million. The Newport zoning board approved conversion into 152 traditional one-bedroom hotel units, enabling significant density uplift. The timeshare was dissolved in 2021, and the listing emphasizes the entitlement's value in unlocking development potential.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily. Entitlement is hotel-use only; no residential multifamily pathway mentioned. If conversion to residential (apartments, condos) is remotely viable, the waterfront location and zoning precedent could signal development opportunity in tight Newport market, but current entitlement is hospitality-focused.

stories.title: Bridge Logistics Properties Acquires 783K-SF Frederickson Distribution Facility
stories.excerpt: Bridge Logistics Properties announced the acquisition of 6920 192nd Street, a 782,775-square-foot distribution facility located in Frederickson, Washington, within the Seattle-Tacoma metro area. The transaction marks BLP’s largest acquisition in the Seattle market to date, further establishing its presence in the Pacific Northwest. Completed in 2024 and fully leased to Harbor Freight Tools on a long-term basis, the facility serves as a regional distribution center supporting its network of more than 1,600 stores nationwide. The property was developed by Panattoni and delivered in 2024 as part of the larger Fred310 industrial development in Frederickson. Jeff Chiate and Bryce Aberg of Cushman & Wakefield facilitated this acquisition. Situated on 53.3 acres, approximately 17 miles from the Port of Tacoma, the largest container port in the Seattle metro area, the property offers exceptional regional connectivity to the ports, major population centers, and critical transportation infrastructure throughout the Pacific Northwest. bullets: Bridge Logistics Properties acquires 782.8K SF Frederickson distribution facility (completed 2024) fully leased to Harbor Freight Tools

stories.summary: Bridge Logistics Properties acquired a 782,775-square-foot distribution facility in Frederickson, Washington (Seattle-Tacoma metro), fully leased to Harbor Freight Tools on long-term basis. The 2024-completed facility on 53.3 acres is BLP's largest Seattle-area acquisition and part of the Fred310 industrial development. Proximity to Port of Tacoma (17 miles) and major transportation infrastructure supports Harbor Freight's 1,600+ store network.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily. However, logistics tenants' consolidation in Seattle-Tacoma region signals sustained warehouse job growth and in-migration of supply-chain workers to Pacific Northwest. Multifamily developers should monitor worker population influx and affordability pressures in Tacoma/Olympia submarkets and consider build-to-rent or workforce housing near emerging logistics clusters.

stories.title: Global Warehouse Tenant Leases Nearly 1.3M SF in Visalia
stories.excerpt: Industrial investor and developer CapRock Partners announced that Building 1 at CapRock Central Point III in Visalia has been fully leased to an undisclosed global corporate tenant. The 1,270,750-square-foot commitment ranks among the largest industrial lease transactions completed in California’s Central Valley in recent years. Located at 4001 N. Plaza Dr., Building 1 represents the first building within CapRock Central Point III, a four-building, 2.7-million-square-foot speculative industrial development. The project is part of CapRock’s larger five-million-square-foot, LEED-certified Central Point master plan. “Today’s occupiers are looking for strategic locations that can help them move faster, operate more efficiently and scale with confidence,” said Monique Snowden, VP of asset management at CapRock. “Visalia delivers a rare combination of access, labor and capacity, and this Building 1 lease further validates the Central Valley’s emergence as a prime logistics hub serving the West Coast and beyond.” The lease was facilitated by JLL executive managing director Mike Fowler and his partners Mike McCrary and Mac Hewett. Lease terms were undisclosed. The post Global Warehouse Tenant Leases Nearly 1.3M SF in Visalia appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CapRock Partners leases 1.27M SF (Building 1, CapRock Central Point III) to undisclosed global corporate tenant in Visalia

Visalia's labor, access, and logistics capacity validate Central Valley emergence as West Coast prime hub
stories.summary: CapRock Partners' Building 1 at CapRock Central Point III in Visalia, California, was fully leased in a 1,270,750-square-foot commitment to an undisclosed global corporate tenant. The transaction ranks among the largest industrial leases in California's Central Valley. The lease validates Visalia's emerging status as a prime logistics hub serving the West Coast, driven by labor availability, access, and capacity.
stories.impact: Central Valley's dominance as a logistics and warehousing hub signals sustained population and wage-worker in-migration to Visalia and surrounding markets. Multifamily developers should evaluate Visalia, Fresno, and nearby markets for workforce housing demand; major industrial tenants anchor employment centers with immediate need for attainable rental stock to attract and retain supply-chain labor.

stories.title: KITA Launches $200M Repositioning of 460 Park Ave.
stories.excerpt: The Korea International Trade Association (KITA) is launching a comprehensive, $200-million redevelopment to reposition 460 Park Ave. as a next-generation office destination. A JLL team led by vice chairmen Dave Kleiner, Frank Doyle and Cynthia Wasserberger and SVP Michael Pallas will handle marketing and leasing for the property. “We are reimagining 460 Park Ave. with a focus on quality, performance and experience, delivering a workplace defined by natural light, modern infrastructure and thoughtfully integrated indoor-outdoor space,” said president Jimin Paik of the Hahn Kook Center, a KITA affiliate. “The result will be a boutique workplace of enduring quality that reflects the prestige and purpose of Park Avenue itself.” The project, which is targeting LEED Gold, WELL certification and WiredScore Platinum, was selected as the third awardee for the Manhattan Commercial Revitalization Program (M-CORE), an initiative designed to promote the transformation of properties in the city’s commercial business districts. The post KITA Launches $200M Repositioning of 460 Park Ave. appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: KITA (Korea International Trade Association) launches $200M repositioning of 460 Park Ave., Manhattan office tower
Project targets LEED Gold, WELL, WiredScore Platinum; selected for M-CORE (Manhattan Commercial Revitalization Program)

stories.summary: The Korea International Trade Association (KITA) is undertaking a $200 million redevelopment of 460 Park Avenue in Manhattan to reposition it as a next-generation office destination. The project targets LEED Gold, WELL certification, and WiredScore Platinum certification and was selected as a third awardee of the Manhattan Commercial Revitalization Program (M-CORE). Focus emphasizes quality, performance, natural light, and integrated indoor-outdoor space.
stories.impact: M-CORE designation and $200M-plus office repositioning in Manhattan CBD suggest landlord/capital confidence in office recovery in prestige Park Avenue corridor. May indicate tech/AI tenant demand and white-collar job concentration in Manhattan, supporting rental demand in residential submarkets adjacent to Park Avenue, Midtown South, and high-amenity CBD neighborhoods—but office-led recovery remains uncertain and slower than multifamily absorption.

stories.title: Grun Group Files Plans for Pair of 99-Unit Residential Buildings in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment and development firm Grun Group has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to bring a pair of 99-unit residential towers to the Bronx’s Woodlawn Heights neighborhood, records show. If approved, the first of the two new buildings will be at 4241 Webster Avenue and span 59,611 square feet. This development will have 99 units across eight floors. The second building will be in the same neighborhood at 4230 Peters Place, spanning 68,733 square feet and also with 99 units. The properties are currently both parking lots. The DOB plans do not provide much more information. Grun Group did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Developers have been busy in the Bronx as of late. Catholic Homes, an affiliate of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of New York, recently secured $146.9 million in construction financing to build affordable housing at 484 East 178th Street in the Bronx. Meanwhile, the city closed on $214 million in financing to bring 288 affordable senior units to 3728 Park Avenue, while housing developer Vilson Lumaj is planning two 99-unit residential properties at 761-769 East Tremont Avenue. Grun Group itself has lately been working on several projects in the city. In Kew Gardens, Queens, Grun Group filed plans in June to build a nine-story, 108-unit residential building at 116-18 Grosnevor Lane. And in January, the firm submitted an application to construct a 94-unit apartment building at 469 Troy Avenue in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Though unconfirmed, it is probable that Grun opted to build two 99-unit residentials at its new project in Woodlawn Heights as a way to take advantage of the city’s 485-x tax abatement program. Limiting the size of a project allows developers to reap the tax benefits of 485-x without paying the high construction wages required when building 100 or more units. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: Grun Group filed plans with NYC Department of Buildings for two 99-unit residential towers in the Bronx's Woodlawn Heights neighborhood. Recent activity includes Catholic Homes securing $146.9 million and the city closing $214 million in affordable housing financing in the Bronx.
stories.impact: Grun Group's dual 99-unit filings in Woodlawn Heights, combined with Catholic Homes and city affordable financing, signal sustained Bronx multifamily development momentum. Modest-sized projects (under 200 units each) suggest build costs and financing remain feasible; Woodlawn Heights location (near 4 train, Yankee Stadium) indicates transit-oriented density is achievable. Monitor zoning approvals and financing conditions as indicator of development velocity and capital availability for Bronx market.

stories.title: Dedeaux Properties CEO Brett Dedeaux On SoCal’s Evergreen Industrial Pull

CEO Brett Dedeaux spoke with Commercial Observer about why the firm sees Tejon Ranch as such a compelling alternative to Los Angeles County and the Inland Empire, as well as how the state’s regulations can add value to entitlements, and why the company remains committed to its home turf. The following is the second of a two-part conversation, and has been edited for length and clarity. Click here for the first part. That performed well, and we sold it to an owner-user in 2024, and that led to a broader joint venture with Tejon Ranch to build out more industrial space. Labor is a big part of the appeal for any logistics company. There is affordable labor and more affordable housing in Tejon Ranch. We kind of say, “Tejon Ranch is the Texas of California.” It is a very business-friendly environment where things get done relatively quickly. It is not as overly regulated. bullets: Dedeaux Properties pursues Tejon Ranch (north of Los Angeles) as alternative to LA County/Inland Empire for industrial
Tejon Ranch offers affordable labor, affordable housing, and lower development friction than coastal CA markets

Labor availability and workforce housing affordability are central to the value proposition.
stories.impact: Dedeaux's pivot to Tejon Ranch signals California's regulatory burden and high development costs are driving industrial capital and logistics investment away from traditional LA/IE corridors. For multifamily: workforce housing demand will follow logistics jobs to Tejon Ranch and northern Kern County; affordable housing and labor-workforce rents will be key to attracting and retaining supply-chain workers in emerging logistics hubs. Consider Tehachapi, Bakersfield, and Kern County submarkets as emerging demand centers.

stories.title: Widening Influence Marked Lisa Pendergast’s Decade Leading CRE Finance Council
stories.excerpt: A decade ago, Lisa Pendergast was enjoying her role heading up commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) strategy at financial giant Jefferies when words of encouragement set her off on a new career path. Pendergast, who at the time had nearly 30 years of capital markets experience under her belt, was urged to apply to lead the Commercial Real Estate Finance Council (CREFC), the trade group she had previously chaired. “A bunch of people said, ‘Lisa, this might be something you want to do,’ and I remember being really angry with them and pounding sand since I really loved my research job,” said Pendergast, who was head of CMBS strategy and risk in Jefferies’ fixed-income line from 2009 to 2016. “I talked to my husband and he was like, ‘You’ve been a member of CREFC, you were chair of CREFC, and you really love this organization,’ and it took me about three months to say I would talk to them and see how it goes.” Prendergast quickly embraced the opportunity. She began her leadership post with the advocacy organization for the CRE finance industry in September 2016 as executive director. Her titles changed to president and CEO in early 2025. She had previously served as CREFC’s chair in 2010 and 2011, and was a member of its board of governors for more than nine years. After nearly 10 years of captaining CREFC through myriad market cycles and challenges, Pendergast will be retiring from the leadership post effective Aug. 3. CREFC’s board of directors is still interviewing potential replacements. Filling Pendergast’s shoes will be far from easy given the strides made during her run at the top, including guiding a 30 percent membership increase while firmly establishing the organization as an influential voice for a range of CRE issues in Washington, D.C., and beyond. In addition to her role at Jefferies, Pendergast, who throughout her CRE finance career was consistently ranked as a top research analyst, also held senior positions at Royal Bank of Scotland and Prudent
bullets: Lisa Pendergast led CRE Finance Council (CREFC) for decade as head of advocacy for CRE finance industry

stories.summary: Lisa Pendergast served as CEO of the Commercial Real Estate Finance Council (CREFC) for a decade, leading the trade advocacy organization after a 30-year career in CMBS strategy and risk at Jefferies. She began her CREFC tenure in September 2016 after initial reluctance. The article chronicles her influence in shaping CRE finance policy and market dynamics.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development and market signals. Profile is retrospective on personnel; no new capital markets, financing conditions, or rate/spread data provided. Monitor CREFC policy positions separately for CMBS market health, loan defaults, and refinancing risk that could signal distress or capital constraints in multifamily sector.
